Putnam County, NY
• Putnam County is included in the New York–Newark–Jersey City,
NY–NJ–PA Metropolitan Statistical Area. It is located in the lower
Hudson River Valley, approximately one hour north of Manhattan.
According to the 2020 Census, there were 97,668 people and 38,713
households in the county.
• The county has several passenger trains that serve the county. The
Harlem Line and the Hudson Line of the Metro-North Railroad run
north–south in Putnam. The Harlem Line makes stops at Brewster,
Southeast, and Patterson. The Hudson Line makes stops at Manitou,
Garrison, Cold Spring, and Breakneck Ridge. Grand Central Terminal
in Manhattan is roughly a one-hour train ride.
• Putnam County has no airport.
• Putnam Area Rapid Transit, also known as PART, is operated by the
county and provides local public transportation.

Putnam Area Rapid Transit
• PART operates four fixed routes year-round in addition to a seasonal
trolley in Cold Spring and a commuter shuttle to the Metro North
Station at Croton Falls.
• PART Paratransit is an origin-to-destination transportation system for
those Putnam residents who are unable to use the PART public
transportation due to a physical or mental disability.

Fixed-route service on large buses offers the economies of scale
that micro-transit lacks until you consider rural suburbia places like
Putnam County. There is an application for this when in Putnam we
are paying $51.93 per ride.
In the context of public transport, the ‘last mile’ is the “provision of
travel service from the nearest public transportation node to a home or
other destination”
Demand Response for Putnam County is a Geographic and
Demographic Solution to better serve the public.

The excitement around micro transit and the idea that public
transportation mimics taxi-like on-demand mobility for the cost
of a regular bus ride is an alluring proposition. Is it right for all
applications?
In an article by David Zipper, December 19, 2023, CityLab –
Perspective titled “On-Demand Microtransit Can’t Escape This Big
Problem” the author claimed that demand response doesn't work. In the
article Mr. Zipper stated that an economist would say that micro transit
does not offer economies of scale: The cost of providing the first rider’s
trip is roughly equal to that of a third, tenth or thousandth rider. Those
costs can be significant. In Los Angeles, for example, a micro transit ride
costs passengers only $1, but each one receives a $42 subsidy.
